 Portable Power Station for WiFi Router Backup: Keep Internet Running During Outages
 16/07/2026 | Anker 
 Blog Center Home Power Backup Portable Power Station Outdoor Solar 
 All 
 Quick answer 
 Start with runtime, not output size. Once your modem and router are within the power station's wattage limit, the battery capacity decides how long your WiFi can stay on. 
 For router-only backup, avoid oversizing for appliances you do not plan to run. Choose enough watt-hours for your target outage window, then add a small reserve. 
 If a brief router reboot would be a problem, choose a model with UPS support and test the setup in advance, before you need it during an outage. 
 A power outage does not always have to mean losing internet access. In many homes, the modem and router use very little electricity, often far less than a laptop, television, or small appliance. With the right portable power station for WiFi router backup, you can keep your connection active for work, school, security cameras, smart home alerts, and basic communication.
 This guide explains why a power station for WiFi router backup is useful, how to estimate runtime, which features matter most, and how to build a setup that fits your home.
 Why Do You Need a Portable Power Station for a WiFi Router? 
 What Features Matter in a Portable Power Station for WiFi Backup? 
 Best Portable Power Station Setup for WiFi Router Backup 
 How to Size a Portable Power Station for a Fridge, Router, and Lights 
 What Capacity Do You Need for a Fridge, Router, and Lights? 
 Recommended Portable Power Station for WiFi Router Backup 
 Conclusion 
 FAQ 
 Why Do You Need a Portable Power Station for a WiFi Router?
 You need a portable power station for a WiFi router because it can keep your home network powered when utility electricity fails. Since routers, modems, and fiber ONTs usually draw modest power, they are among the easiest devices to support with battery backup.
 Keep Your Internet Connection During Power Outages
 A portable power station can keep your modem and router running when the grid goes down, as long as your internet provider’s local equipment remains active. Many routers use around 5 to 20 watts, while modems may use a similar amount. Together, a typical home network may draw roughly 15 to 40 watts.
 Support Remote Work and Online Productivity
 For remote workers, a power station keeps the WiFi router running during storms or rolling blackouts. It protects video calls, cloud documents, payments, and customer messages, while giving you time to save work, update teammates, finish meetings, or switch hotspots. A few backup hours can preserve deadlines and business continuity.
 Maintain Smart Home and Security Devices
 Smart home security relies on WiFi. When a router loses power, cameras, locks, sensors, and alarms may stop alerting or recording, even with charged batteries. A power station can keep the network online, support phones for notifications, and power key hubs or storage, so estimate all essential devices before outages.
 Avoid Noisy and Inconvenient Generator Alternatives
 Gas generators suit heavy loads, but they are noisy, need fuel, must stay outdoors, and are excessive for routers. A portable power station is cleaner, quieter, exhaust-free, and starts instantly indoors nearby. For apartments, rentals, or suburban homes, battery backup keeps WiFi running safely without outdoor cords or generator hassle.
 What Features Matter in a Portable Power Station for WiFi Backup?
 If you are comparing a portable power station with WiFi app control, remember that app features are convenient but not a substitute for the right capacity and output options. Start with your devices, then match the station to your actual needs.
 UPS Function for Uninterrupted Internet Access
 A UPS function allows the power station to keep devices running when grid power fails. In a typical setup, the station stays plugged into the wall, and your modem and router plug into the station. When utility power drops, the battery takes over quickly.
 For remote work, this feature can be valuable because it reduces the chance of your router rebooting during a call. Transfer times vary by model, so check the specifications.
 Some networking devices tolerate brief interruptions better than others, but faster switching is usually better. If you depend on live video calls, security monitoring, or smart home access, UPS support can make the backup setup feel much more seamless.
 Enough Capacity for Your Entire Emergency Setup
 Capacity is measured in watt-hours, or Wh. A higher Wh rating usually means longer runtime. For WiFi-only backup, many households can start with a compact or mid-size model. For a modem, router, laptop, phone charging, and a few lights, a larger power station makes more sense.
 A rough estimate is simple. Add the wattage of your devices, then multiply by the number of hours you want. Add extra margin for AC conversion loss and battery reserve.
 This helps avoid buying a unit that looks adequate but runs short too soon. For example, a 30W network setup for 10 hours requires about 300Wh before losses, so choosing extra capacity improves reliability.
 Long-Lasting LFP Battery Chemistry 
 LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries are widely used in modern power stations because they offer long cycle life and stable performance. For home backup, that matters because the battery may sit charged for long periods, then be used repeatedly during outages or storm seasons. 
 Compared with older lithium-ion chemistries, LFP designs are known for durability and thermal stability. They can be slightly heavier for the same capacity, but for household backup, the tradeoff is often worthwhile. 
 A longer-lasting battery can deliver better value over years of use. This is especially important if you plan to keep the station plugged in, recharge it often, or use it as part of a regular emergency preparedness setup. 
 Multiple Charging Options
 A good WiFi backup power station should be easy to recharge before and during an emergency. AC wall charging is fastest in many cases, but solar and vehicle charging add flexibility when the grid stays down.
 Look at charging input, not just battery size. A large battery with very slow charging may be frustrating during short windows of available power.
 If you expect repeated outages, faster AC charging and meaningful solar input can make the system much more practical in real life. Multiple charging options also let you adapt to changing conditions, such as using wall power before a storm and solar power afterward.
 Best Portable Power Station Setup for WiFi Router Backup
 The best portable power station setup for WiFi router backup depends on what you need to keep online. A simple setup may power only the modem and router, while a larger setup can support work devices, phones, lights, and household essentials.
 Simple WiFi-Only Backup Setup
 A simple WiFi-only backup setup usually includes a modem, router, and possibly a fiber ONT. These devices plug directly into the power station’s AC outlets. If your router supports compatible DC input, using DC output may reduce conversion loss, but most household users will find AC easier.
 This setup works well for storms, short outages, and basic connectivity. It is also easy to test.
 Plug in the networking devices, check the displayed wattage, and calculate runtime based on the station’s remaining capacity. If your total draw is low, you may be able to keep messaging, weather alerts, and smart home notifications active for an extended period.
 Work-From-Home Backup Setup
 A work-from-home setup should support both internet access and the tools needed to stay productive. At a minimum, that may include your modem, router, laptop, phone, and a small LED light. If you use a monitor, docking station, or desktop computer, your power needs rise significantly.
 For many users, a mid-size station is the better choice because it avoids constant power management. If uninterrupted service matters, choose a model with UPS support and keep your router connected through it during work hours.
 This setup helps you handle brief outages without losing meetings or documents. It also gives you time to decide whether to continue working, conserve battery, or switch to mobile data.
 Home Emergency Backup Setup
 A home emergency setup is designed for longer outages and shared household needs. It may power WiFi continuously while rotating other loads, such as phone chargers, lights, a radio, or a refrigerator. You do not have to run every device all day.
 The best strategy is to assign priorities. Keep communication and safety devices online first, then use remaining capacity for comfort.
 A larger power station WiFi backup plan can also include solar charging, giving you a way to extend runtime when grid power is unavailable. This is useful for families that need reliable communication during storms, wildfire shutoffs, or winter weather events.
 How to Size a Portable Power Station for a Fridge, Router, and Lights 
 A refrigerator, router, and a few lights can run from one portable power station when the total load stays within the station's output rating and the battery has enough usable watt-hours. The most useful way to size this setup is to add the running watts first, then check the refrigerator's starting watts before choosing capacity. 
 Add Up the Wattage 
 Use the table below as a planning estimate. Actual power draw changes by appliance size, age, room temperature, thermostat setting, door openings, and the equipment plugged into your network. 
 Device 
 Planning wattage 
 What to check before an outage 
 Refrigerator 
 About 150W cycling average 
 Check the appliance label or manual for running watts and starting watts. 
 Refrigerator startup surge 
 About 2-3 times running watts 
 Make sure the power station can handle the compressor's short startup demand. 
 Router + modem 
 About 15-20W typical, up to 40W for higher-draw setups 
 Add the router, modem, and fiber ONT if your home uses one. 
 3 LED lights 
 About 30W total 
 Count only the lights you plan to use during the outage. 
 For this example, the combined running load is about 195 to 200W in a typical setup before conversion loss. If your router, modem, and fiber ONT are closer to the top of the range, plan for more margin instead of treating 200W as a fixed result. Food timing also matters during a long outage. The FDA's guidance on food safety during power outages says an unopened refrigerator can keep food cold for about 4 hours, while a full freezer can hold temperature for about 48 hours if the door stays closed. Choosing a more efficient refrigerator can reduce the load as well, since ENERGY STAR explains how ENERGY STAR certified refrigerators use less power by about 9% compared with models that meet the federal minimum standard. 
 Convert to Watt-Hours You Can Plan For 
 Once the running watts are clear, convert the load into watt-hours. The basic runtime estimate is: 
 Capacity (Wh) × 0.9 ÷ Load (W) = Runtime (hours) 
 The 0.9 factor leaves room for inverter loss and practical battery reserve. With a 200W combined load, plan for about 220Wh of battery capacity for each hour you want the refrigerator, router, and lights to run together. For a 6-hour window, that means roughly 1,330Wh before adding any extra devices. For a refrigerator-only setup, our guide to how much power a refrigerator needs during an outage can help you check fridge runtime before adding router and lighting loads. Our guide to what a watt-hour means for backup planning explains the unit in simpler terms. 
 What Capacity Do You Need for a Fridge, Router, and Lights? 
 For this combined load, capacity decides runtime after you confirm output and surge support. The table below uses the same 195 to 200W typical load range from the example above, which covers a refrigerator cycling average, a modem and router, and three LED lights. 
 Capacity Tiers for This Combined Load 
 The figures below use official Anker SOLIX capacity specs and the runtime formula above. They are planning estimates, not lab-test results.

 Longer essential backup when you want more room for router runtime, lighting, and careful refrigerator cycling.

 If you want to test your own appliance list, our Anker SOLIX Power Runtime Estimator can help you compare different loads before you choose a capacity tier. Keep the refrigerator's starting watts in mind. A power station may have enough watt-hours for runtime but still be the wrong match if its output cannot handle the compressor's short startup surge. 
 When One Tier Isn't Enough 
 One power station can often cover a refrigerator, WiFi router, and a few lights, but longer outages change the daily energy need quickly. A second refrigerator, a freezer, a fan, or laptop charging can push your total load higher than the table shows. 
 For households that want more time or more reserve, Anker SOLIX F3800 can connect with Anker SOLIX BP3800 Expansion Batteries for a larger backup setup. Keep this decision tied to your actual essentials. If the goal is food safety, communication, and basic lighting, start with those loads first, then add comfort devices only after you know how much runtime remains. 
 Recommended Portable Power Station for WiFi Router Backup
 The best recommended model depends on whether you want basic internet backup or broader home resilience. For WiFi alone, focus on runtime, outlets, and convenience. For longer outages, choose a system with more capacity and stronger expansion potential.
 You can compare broader options in the portable power stations collection, especially if you are balancing router backup with phones, laptops, lights, and other emergency devices.
 Anker SOLIX S5000: Best for Long-Lasting Essential Home Backup 
 For households that want to keep WiFi and essential appliances running through longer outages, the Anker SOLIX S5000  offers a plug-and-play home backup solution. It combines long runtime with flexible power support, making it suitable for keeping everyday essentials running without a complex whole-home installation.

 Anker SOLIX S2000 Portable Power Station: Best for WiFi and Essential Home Backup
 For users who mainly want to keep their internet connection, communication devices, and essential electronics running during an outage, the Anker SOLIX S2000 Portable Power Station is a practical choice. Its 2,010Wh capacity and 314Ah LFP cells provide reliable backup power for low-consumption devices such as WiFi routers, modems, laptops, and LED lights, making it well suited for remote workers, apartment residents, and families preparing for short-to-medium power interruptions.

 Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus Portable Power Station: Best for Extended Home Backup
 For homeowners who need more than just WiFi backup, the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus Portable Power Station is designed for longer outages and higher-power applications. With a larger battery capacity, higher output, and expandable storage, it can support essential home circuits, RV equipment, and larger appliances when extended backup power is needed.
 3,840Wh battery capacity to provide longer runtime for essential devices
 6,000W AC output to handle higher-power appliances and demanding loads
 120V/240V dual-voltage output for greater home and RV compatibility
 Expandable capacity up to 53.8kWh for extended energy storage needs
 Solar charging support for off-grid and emergency energy replenishment
 Conclusion
 A portable power station for WiFi router backup is one of the simplest ways to stay connected during a blackout. Because routers and modems usually use modest power, even a compact station can provide useful runtime. A larger unit can support your full work setup, phones, lights, and other essentials.
 UPS support is worth considering if uninterrupted internet matters for work, security systems, or smart home access. Solar and vehicle charging are also helpful when outages last longer than expected. These features turn a simple battery into a more flexible backup system.
 FAQ
 How long will a portable power station run a WiFi router?
 A portable power station can power a WiFi router for hours. Runtime depends on usable battery watt-hours and total device wattage. Add router and modem watts, then divide capacity by load. A 500Wh unit running 25W may last 15–18 hours.
 Can I power both a modem and a router with one battery?
 Yes, one portable power station can run a modem, router, and fiber ONT if it has enough outlets and capacity. Add each device’s wattage, estimate desired runtime, and choose a station with an extra safety margin. Always use compatible adapters safely.
 Is a power bank enough for a WiFi router?
 Most USB power banks cannot run a home WiFi router unless it accepts USB-C power or a matching DC voltage. Many routers require 12V via a barrel adapter. A portable power station is safer, offering AC outlets and compatible DC options.
 Will my internet still work if the neighborhood loses power?
 Your home WiFi may work during an outage if your modem, router, and your internet provider’s local infrastructure still have power. A portable power station can keep your home equipment running, but it cannot control the provider’s network, street-level equipment, or damaged lines. Cable, fiber, and fixed wireless services vary by area. Keep mobile data as a backup if internet access is critical.
 How many watt-hours do I need to run a refrigerator, router, and lights together during an outage? 
 Plan for about 220Wh per hour for a refrigerator, router, and a few LED lights. This uses a typical 195 to 200W combined load, with margin for conversion loss and battery reserve. For 6 hours, plan around 1,330Wh before adding other devices. Check your refrigerator label and router adapter because wattage varies by model, age, room temperature, and door openings. 
 Can one portable power station handle a fridge, WiFi router, and a few lights at the same time? 
 Yes, one portable power station can handle a fridge, WiFi router, and a few lights if it has enough capacity for your target runtime and enough surge output for the fridge compressor. The typical running load may be about 195 to 200W, but startup demand can briefly reach 2-3 times the fridge's running watts. Check both numbers before relying on the setup during an outage.

How to Keep Wi-Fi Running During a Power Outage | Outage Ready Home 
 Internet Backup Guide
 How to Keep Wi-Fi Running During a Power Outage
 Wi-Fi can keep working during a power outage if your router and modem have backup power and your internet provider’s network is still online. The best setup depends on how many devices you need to power and how long the outage lasts.
 Use Wi-Fi Runtime Calculator Power Station Guide 
 Router and modem backup
 Useful for remote work and students
 Test before the outage happens
 Guide Status

 Quick Navigation

 Calculate Wi-Fi Runtime Quick Answer
 How Can You Keep Wi-Fi Working During an Outage?
 To keep Wi-Fi running during a power outage, power both the router and modem with a backup battery, mini UPS or portable power station. A small router UPS may work for short outages, while a portable power station is better if you also need a laptop, phone charger or light.
 Best Ways to Keep Wi-Fi Running
 The right option depends on whether you only need internet equipment or a larger home office setup.
 Portable Power Station
 Router, modem, laptop and longer backup
 A portable power station is one of the most flexible options because it can power a router, modem, laptop, phone charger and small light at the same time.
 Mini UPS for Router
 Router-only or modem-router backup
 A small router UPS can keep internet equipment running through short outages without needing a large battery.
 USB-C Power Bank
 Compatible routers and small setups
 Some routers can run from USB-C or DC power with the right cable or adapter, making a power bank useful for compact backup.
 Full Home UPS
 Desktop, router, modem and office gear
 A larger UPS can support a desktop setup briefly, but runtime may be limited if the load is high.
 Simple Wi-Fi Backup Setup Steps
 Before buying anything, figure out exactly which internet devices need power.
 01
 Find out what needs power
 Check whether your home internet needs only a router, or both a modem and router. Many homes need both powered at the same time.
 02
 Estimate the total watts
 Add the router watts, modem watts and any extra devices such as a laptop, light or phone charger.
 03
 Choose a backup battery
 Use a power station, mini UPS or compatible power bank based on the total load and how many hours of backup you need.
 04
 Test before an outage
 Plug your internet equipment into the backup source and confirm it works before you actually need it.
 Wi-Fi Backup Battery Size Guide
 These are planning ranges. Your actual runtime depends on router wattage, modem wattage, battery efficiency and any extra devices.
 Router only
 150Wh–300Wh
 Typical load: 10W–15W
 Good for short to medium outages if your internet provider stays online.
 Router + modem
 300Wh–500Wh
 Typical load: 20W–35W
 A practical range for many home internet backup setups.
 Router + modem + laptop
 500Wh–1,000Wh
 Typical load: 60W–100W+
 Better for remote work, but runtime drops as laptop load increases.
 Small home office
 1,000Wh+
 Typical load: 100W+
 Useful if you need internet, laptop, lights and small work devices.
 Setup Typical Load Starting Battery Note 
 Router only 10W–15W 150Wh–300Wh Good for short to medium outages if your internet provider stays online. 
 Router + modem 20W–35W 300Wh–500Wh A practical range for many home internet backup setups. 
 Router + modem + laptop 60W–100W+ 500Wh–1,000Wh Better for remote work, but runtime drops as laptop load increases. 
 Small home office 100W+ 1,000Wh+ Useful if you need internet, laptop, lights and small work devices. 
 Common Wi-Fi Backup Mistakes
 ! Powering only the router when the modem also needs backup power.
 ! Assuming internet will work if the provider network is also down.
 ! Running a laptop, monitor and lights from a tiny router backup battery.
 ! Waiting until an outage to test the setup.
 ! Ignoring battery efficiency and conversion losses.
 ! Using high-drain devices from the same backup source unnecessarily.
 Want to Estimate Your Runtime?
 Use the Wi-Fi runtime calculator to estimate how long your router, modem and small home office devices may run from a backup battery.

 FAQ
 Can Wi-Fi work during a power outage?
 Yes, Wi-Fi can work during a power outage if your router and modem have backup power and your internet provider’s network is still operating.
 What is the best way to keep Wi-Fi running during an outage?
 For many homes, a small portable power station or router UPS is the easiest option. A power station is more flexible because it can also power a laptop, phone charger or light.
 How many watts does a Wi-Fi router use?
 Many routers use roughly 10 to 20 watts, but the exact number depends on the model. A separate modem can add more power draw.
 Can a power bank run a Wi-Fi router?
 Sometimes. It depends on the router’s power input and whether you have a compatible USB-C, DC or adapter setup. Always check the router requirements first.

Router, phones, and lights: a 24-hour outage plan

Written by

casey jenkins

in

Guides

Not every outage plan needs to power the refrigerator. For most short outages, the difference between misery and comfort is smaller: keep the Wi-Fi on, keep the phones charged, keep the lights on, and top up the laptop.

This is the cheapest useful backup setup. The entire plan fits in a ~500Wh portable power station — and for apartment dwellers and skeptics, it’s the best first purchase in backup power.

All runtime figures below are Estimates with assumptions shown. Nothing here is a guaranteed runtime.

Illustrative image — a generic station in a blackout scenario.
Our picks for this guide

Jackery Explorer 500 — The smallest unit that still covers a router for a full day (28–31 hours in our model). Note: Jackery no longer sells the Explorer 500 new; its successor is the HomePower 1000 v2. Previously listed at $299.

Read our analysis

EcoFlow DELTA 3 — 55–61 hours of router runtime, with headroom for phones and lights too.

Check price at Amazon

Buying through affiliate links may earn us a commission.

The loads
Load	Draw (typical)	Hours in the plan
Wi-Fi router	10–12W	24 (running continuously)
2 phones, full charges	~40Wh total	charged as needed
3 LED bulbs	~27W total	3 (evening hours)
Laptop, one full top-up	~65Wh	once during the day
The worked math

Assume 85% inverter efficiency: divide each load’s energy by 0.85 to get the station capacity it consumes.

Load	Energy needed	Station capacity consumed (Estimate)
Router: 10W × 24h	240Wh	282Wh
2 phone charges	40Wh	47Wh
3 LED bulbs: 27W × 3h	81Wh	95Wh
Laptop top-up	65Wh	76Wh
Total		~500Wh

A 518Wh station covers this full 24-hour plan with roughly 18Wh to spare (Estimate) — it fits, but the margin is thin.

Why this is the best first purchase
It’s cheap. The ~500Wh class starts around $300 (price checked 2026-10-15).
It’s apartment-friendly. No fuel, no fumes, no noise — nothing your lease forbids.
It solves the outage you’ll actually have. Most outages are hours, not days.
It teaches you the math. Once you’ve run this kit through one real outage, sizing a fridge-scale station later is easy.
What it won’t run — and why
A refrigerator. A 150W fridge would drain a 518Wh station in about 7 hours (Estimate), consuming the entire kit.
A microwave. ~1,000W+ draw exceeds the 500W continuous output of this class.
A space heater. ~1,500W typical draw — no portable station in this price class runs one.

Those jobs belong to the 1,000Wh+ tiers.

Which ~500Wh station, ranked for this scenario
Jackery Explorer 500 — 518Wh, 500W continuous / 1,000W peak, 13.3 lbs. The only unit in our records in this exact class. Tradeoffs: older NMC chemistry (500 cycles to 80%), ~7.5-hour wall recharge, one AC outlet, no USB-C. Around $299 on Amazon (recheck before buying). Read our analysis Note: Jackery no longer sells the Explorer 500 new; its successor is the HomePower 1000 v2.
BLUETTI AC180 — 1,152Wh, 1,800W continuous, LiFePO4 (3,500+ cycles), 4× AC outlets, 5-year warranty. Roughly double the runtime — run the full plan for 24 hours and still have half the battery left. $449.00 (checked 2026-11-02). Check price at BLUETTI
EcoFlow RIVER 3 — 245Wh, 300W continuous, LiFePO4 (3,000 cycles), 7.8 lbs, sub-20ms UPS mode. Covers about half the scenario — router all day plus phones. Direct price could not be verified today. Read our analysis
Your next step

 Yes, and it is one of the easiest jobs a portable power station can do. A broadband router is a tiny, low-wattage load, so even a compact portable power station can keep it and your Wi-Fi alive for many hours on a single charge.  How Much Power Does a Broadband Router Actually Use?
 Very little, which is why a portable power station handles it so comfortably. A typical router draws only a handful of watts, and its separate fibre modem or ONT adds a little more. Together, the pair is one of the lowest-draw loads in the home, so the same portable power station that struggles with a kettle will happily power your broadband for hour after hour. This modest demand is precisely why a router makes the perfect first device to back up with a portable power station.
 Why Is UPS Switchover the Feature That Matters?
 Because a power cut rarely warns you it is coming. A standard portable power station only helps once you notice the outage and move the plug, but an Anker SOLIX portable power station with UPS support detects the drop in mains and switches to battery almost instantly. Your router, Wi-Fi and any device running through it never blink offline, so a video call, a work session or a smart-home hub carries on uninterrupted. For broadband backup, this switchover is the single most valuable feature a portable power station can offer.
 Which Portable Power Station Tier Suits a Router?
 For broadband alone, a compact portable power station is more than enough, keeping a router and modem online through a full evening outage. Step up to a mid-range portable power station and you can run the router while also covering phone charging, a laptop and a few LED lights. A high-capacity portable power station makes sense only if you want broadband to be one part of a larger whole-home backup plan. Anker SOLIX offers a portable power station for every one of these ambitions.
 What Else Should You Plug In Alongside the Router?
 Think of your portable power station as the centre of a small connectivity hub. Beyond the router and its modem, add the devices that keep a household functioning: a phone on charge, a laptop, a reading lamp and perhaps a smart speaker or baby monitor. Keep the total load modest and the portable power station will stretch its stored energy much further. Reserve the heavier appliances for later, and let the portable power station focus on the quiet essentials first.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 Will a portable power station keep my Wi-Fi running in a power cut?
 Yes. A router draws very little power, so a portable power station keeps your Wi-Fi online for hours. For seamless backup, choose a portable power station with UPS pass-through so the connection never drops when the mains fails.
 How long can a portable power station run a router?
 A compact portable power station typically runs a router for a full evening and often much longer, because the load is only a few watts. Runtime depends on the tier of portable power station and the router's exact draw.
 What does UPS pass-through mean for a router?
 UPS pass-through lets a portable power station stay plugged in and switch to battery almost instantly when mains power fails, with no interruption. It is the key feature to look for when backing up a router or home office.
 Do I need to plug the modem in too?
 Yes. Your broadband needs both the router and its modem or fibre ONT, so plug both into the same portable power station. If only the router has power, there is no signal for the portable power station to share over Wi-Fi.
 Is a compact portable power station enough for broadband?
 For broadband alone, yes. A compact portable power station covers a router and modem comfortably. Move up to a mid-range portable power station if you also want to run a laptop, phone and lighting at the same time.
 Can I leave a portable power station plugged in for the router?
 Yes, and you should. An Anker SOLIX portable power station with a BMS manages charging safely, so leaving it connected through UPS pass-through means the portable power station protects your router the instant the power drops.
